claims.text: The initial material is an equiatomic FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy with an FCC crystal structure.
The initial FeNiCrMn structure contains pre-existing vacancy clusters.
The initial FeNiCrMn structure contains atomic-scale chemical short-range order.
Vacancy clusters are the primary nucleation sites for Shockley partial dislocations in FeNiCrMn.
Shockley partial dislocations create intrinsic stacking faults with HCP-like local coordination but no long-range HCP periodicity.
Dislocation nucleation requires thermal activation to break local chemical order at vacancy clusters and form a stacking fault.
The local-order nucleation barrier, rather than dislocation glide velocity, is the rate-limiting step for yielding.
At high strain rates, dislocation density increases because insufficient time is available for dislocation annihilation.
Dominance of the thermally activated nucleation barrier makes the macroscopic yield strength insensitive to strain rate between 10^8 and 10^10 s^-1.
Yield strength remains constant across strain rates from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
Yield strength decreases monotonically as temperature increases.
The <11-1> orientation has a geometrically harder partial-dislocation slip system than the <110> orientation.
The <11-1> orientation requires a higher critical resolved shear stress for Shockley-partial nucleation than <110>.
The <11-1> orientation will exhibit a 5–15% higher yield stress than the <110> orientation.
The observed HCP-like regions are transient intrinsic stacking faults stabilized by local chemical short-range order rather than a true phase transformation.
A lack of volume change supports identifying the HCP-like regions as stacking faults rather than a transformed HCP phase.
The HCP-like regions will lack the long-range translational symmetry of a true HCP phase.
The ideal HCP c/a ratio is stated as 1.633 or 8/3.
A distorted local c/a ratio together with absent long-range HCP symmetry can discriminate a stacking fault from a true HCP transformation.
The proposed mechanism applies only while thermal activation dominates and fails in a purely athermal regime or after thermal randomization of short-range order.

contradictions.description: The text treats 1.633 and 8/3 as interchangeable ideal HCP c/a ratios, but 8/3 is approximately 2.667; the ideal ratio is sqrt(8/3), approximately 1.633.
